poll.title: Preseason poll
poll.note: Four desks, four full ballots, twelve points for a first-place vote down to one. Nothing has been played, so this is entirely opinion and it gets counted like the college polls.

ballots.comment: I submitted the projection order and I will not be apologising for it. But understand what that order is worth: ten of these teams sit inside 8.3 points a week of each other. My slots two through ten are a coin flip wearing a suit. The only two entries I would defend under questioning are the bottom two, and I would defend those vigorously.

Kevin over Killian at the top, by the width of a hair. A 2.5 point weekly edge is not a reason to hand anyone a first-place vote, so I broke the tie on roster construction rather than the projection. Jack sits tenth on my ballot because his is the oldest roster in the league at 27.6 years, and age is the one number in this sport that only moves one direction.

Brian first. He built a team and then left it alone, which in this league counts as discipline. Chris is eleventh and he can take that up with the starting quarterback he released for free. And Killian is fifth, because I am not handing the top spot in my poll to a projection model. Projections do not play defense. Projections have never been punched in the mouth.

Jake first, Jerey second, and no I will not be explaining the methodology. Here is what I will explain. Every number in this poll comes from a projection of a game that has not happened, generated by a company that also wants you to click on a betting line. Odessa built her whole ballot on it. I built mine on spite. Come find me in December and we will compare.

stories.headline: Five managers bid, three have not touched their roster all season
stories.body:
A week after this desk complained that twelve hundred dollars of FAAB was sitting untouched, five managers placed bids and three of them fought over the same receiver. Caleb Douglas went to Jack for $11. Adam bid $8. Jomi bid $6.

The full budgets are misleading, so here is the actual split. Jack has spent $11, Justin $7, Adam and Jomi $6 each. Trevor also bid, $5 on the Tampa Bay defense, and lost it to Jomi by a single dollar, which costs nothing and is why he still shows a hundred. Four more moved without spending at all: Killian added Dalton Schultz, Jake added Keaton Mitchell, Jeff added Devaughn Vele and Chris added Tre Tucker, all free once a player clears waivers.

That leaves three managers who have made no transaction of any kind since the draft: Jerey, Kevin and Brian. Two of them are 1-0, and one of those two posted the highest score in the league.
stories.storyline: Five managers have bid on waivers and four more have added free agents. Jerey, Kevin and Brian have made no transaction of any kind since the draft. Open question: whether doing nothing keeps working for the two of them who are 1-0.

takes.text: Three men have not touched their rosters since draft night. Not a bid, not a pickup, nothing! And two of them are 1-0, and one of them put up the highest score in this league. Do not tell me that is a strategy. That is a man who got lucky and has not noticed yet.

The interesting bid is Trevor's. He lost the Tampa Bay defense by one dollar, which is the cheapest possible way to lose an auction and the most avoidable. If you value a player at five you do not bid five, you bid six. This is the entire theory of blind bidding and it costs nothing to learn.

The full budget figure is the wrong thing to read. Eight teams have a hundred dollars and only three of them have been idle. Trevor bid and lost by a dollar, which is activity, and four others took free agents at no cost, which is also activity. Spending is not the same as paying attention.

Somebody in this league paid eleven American dollars, of an imaginary hundred, for a wide receiver most of you have never heard of. Fantasy football is back and it is exactly as glamorous as I remembered.

stories.headline: Adam is trading away the player his team is named after
stories.body:
A trade has been agreed and not yet processed: Jalen Coker to Chris, Mike Evans to Adam. One for one.

The joke writes itself. Adam runs Coker? I hardly know her! Jalen Coker scored 33.80 for him in week one against an 11.9 projection, the best individual performance on any losing roster that week and the second largest overperformance in the league. He is now leaving, and the team name is going nowhere.

On the numbers it is close to even for week two. Coker projects 12.9, Evans 13.7. Chris was starting Evans; Adam was starting Coker. The difference is that Chris now owns three players his own team is named after or around, and Adam owns none of his.
stories.storyline: Adam has agreed to trade Jalen Coker to Chris for Mike Evans, pending processing. Adam's team is named after Coker. Open question: whether Adam renames the team, and which side the points end up favouring.

takes.text: Coker? I hardly know her! is about to become literally true. He will hardly know her. She plays for Chris now. I have waited my entire career for a transaction this stupid and I want everyone to understand I mean that as praise.

Straight one for one with projections 0.8 apart is as close to a neutral trade as this league is likely to produce. The case for Adam is that Evans is the steadier of the two; the case against is that he just traded the player who outscored his projection by 21.9 points four days ago.

You do not trade the guy the team is named after! That is not a roster move, that is an identity crisis conducted in public! And he is getting back a receiver worth eight tenths of a point more! For the whole week!

Ignore the name and it is a defensible swap between a 1-0 team and an 0-1 team who both start the position. The thing worth watching is that Adam projects last in the league this week and this trade does not change that. It is a lateral move by the team that needed a vertical one.

stories.headline: Chris is starting Isaiah Likely this week and has benched Deebo Samuel
stories.body:
Last week I'sah Likely to win Deebo won a game while leaving 27.80 points from Isaiah Likely on the bench and starting Colston Loveland for nothing. This week Likely is in the lineup, listed at tight end and now with the Giants, projected 9.3. Loveland starts as well at 12.0.

The move that raises an eyebrow is the other half of the team name. Deebo Samuel, who scored 18.00 against a 10.1 projection and was the story of week one, is on the bench for week two.

Chris is 1-0 with 79 percent playoff odds and faces Brian, who owns the best projected roster in the league this week at 132.9 against Chris's 118.9. It is the second largest projected gap on the slate.
stories.storyline: Chris has moved Isaiah Likely into his lineup and dropped Deebo Samuel to the bench, reversing both halves of last week's arrangement. Open question: whether the namesakes keep deciding his weeks.

takes.text: He benched Likely and won. Now he is starting Likely and benching Deebo. At this rate he will work his way through the entire team name by November and we will finally learn which half of the pun is load-bearing.

This is a defensible correction rather than a joke. Likely has changed clubs and the projection now rates him as a real starter. Benching Deebo after an 18 point week is the harder call, and it is the one I would want explained.

You do not bench the man who won you the week! Eighteen points! Against a ten point projection! And he is on the pine because a spreadsheet likes somebody else by two points. This is how you lose games you were supposed to win.

Ward is being kind. The 27.80 Chris left on the bench last week was nearly twice his margin of victory. Correcting it is not a story, it is the minimum. The Deebo decision is worth 13.7 projected points against alternatives and is genuinely close.

stories.headline: Killian is at 94 percent and this desk has written his obituary twice
stories.body:
Team Ketchup holds 94 percent playoff odds and a 40 percent shot at the top seed, both comfortably the highest in Sigma Pi B. Nobody else is above 83. He projects 132.4 this week, second only to Brian.

Twelve days ago he was tenth in projected strength at 34 percent odds and every desk here wrote about the collapse. Six days ago it turned out that collapse was a tight end with no published projection being counted as zero. Since then he has scored 157.82, added Dalton Schultz, and climbed 60 points of playoff probability without anyone saying much about it.

He plays Jake this week, who has the worst projected total of the two at 110.5 and 14 percent odds. It is the largest projected gap on the week 2 slate at 18.1 points.
stories.storyline: Killian holds 94 percent playoff odds and the best top-seed chance in the league after being written up twice as a collapsing team. Open question: whether anyone catches him.

takes.text: Ninety-four percent in week two is the model saying a 1-0 start plus the second best roster is close to decisive in a twelve team league with six spots. It is not decisive. It is the model having very little to go on and being confident anyway, which is a thing models do.

Worth remembering how much of this rests on one week. He beat Brian by 29 points and jumped 13 points of odds. If the result had flipped, so would the table. I would hold the celebration until there is a second data point.

The invisible trophy is now a 40 percent chance at a real one. I have been covering Killian's death and resurrection for two weeks and at no point has he said a single word to anybody. Model behaviour, frankly.
He gets Jake this week, the man who played a perfect lineup and lost by 43. That is not a matchup, that is a mugging scheduled in advance.

stories.headline: The commissioner's team projects last and his best receiver has no projection at all
stories.body:
Coker? I hardly know her! is bottom of the league in projected strength for week two at 103.0 and holds 4 percent playoff odds, down from 21 percent a week ago. Only Jeff, at 2 percent, is worse.

Part of it is that A.J. Brown has no published projection this week. He appears in the site's missing projections list, substituted at replacement level rather than zero, and sits on Adam's bench. Josh Jacobs is in the same position. Two of the players who were meant to carry that roster currently have no number attached to them at all.

Adam did move on the wire, winning Chris Bell for $6 and losing two other claims. He also draws Justin this week, who projects 15.8 points higher. On the current numbers the commissioner is a 15 point underdog in his own newspaper.
stories.storyline: Adam projects last in the league at 103.0 with 4 percent playoff odds, and two of his key players have no published projection. Open question: whether the roster is actually this bad or the missing data is hiding it.

takes.text: I want to be careful here, because this is exactly the failure that embarrassed us with Killian. A.J. Brown and Josh Jacobs have no published projection. We are substituting replacement level, which is honest, but if either is healthy and playing then Adam's 103.0 is understated and so is the 4 percent.

The man built the website, hired us, gave us the numbers, and the numbers say he is the worst team in the league and a 15 point underdog on Sunday. I want it on record that I have never enjoyed a job more.
Twenty-one percent to four percent in one week! He lost by fifty-four to a team named after him and the model has decided that was the real him. I am not sure it is wrong.

The honest read is that one blowout loss plus two unprojected starters will do this to a number. Jalen Coker scored 33.80 for him last week and projects 12.9 this week. That roster is not last in the league. It is being measured badly.

stories.headline: Week 2 is two coin flips and four mismatches
stories.body:
The projections separate this slate cleanly. Jerey against Trevor is the closest game on the board at 2.8 points, a rematch of nothing in particular between the team that leads the draft card and the team that grades twelfth. Jack against Kevin is next at 5.5.

After that it opens up. Jomi is favoured over Jeff by 12.5, Brian over Chris by 14.0, Justin over Adam by 15.8, and Killian over Jake by 18.1. Four of the six games have a projected gap larger than any matchup produced in week one except the blowouts.

The Book now prices all of this: spreads, totals and moneylines, with picks you can make on your own device. It grades itself once the week finishes.
stories.storyline: Week 2 projects as two close games and four mismatches, the tightest being Jerey against Trevor at 2.8 points. Open question: whether the projected gaps mean anything given week 1's results ignored them.

takes.text: A reminder from last week before anyone treats these as settled. Kevin was projected second and scored the most in the league. Jake was projected eleventh and set a perfect lineup. The projections got the shape roughly right and the order badly wrong.

A 2.8 point projected gap is a coin flip with extra steps. An 18 point gap is roughly a 75 percent favourite once you account for weekly variance, which is a long way from certain. Nobody on this slate is safe and nobody is dead.

Trevor is favoured! Trevor! The man who scored 78 points and left 29 on the bench is a favourite this week, because the same numbers that buried him last Sunday have decided he is fine. Make it make sense.
Four mismatches and two coin flips, and every one of you will lose to somebody you were supposed to beat. I have seen one week of this league and I am already certain.

stories.headline: CORRUPT COMMISSIONER'S NEWSPAPER FINALLY GETS RESULTS, REFUSES TO TAKE CREDIT
stories.body:
Last week this column pointed out that twelve hundred dollars of waiver money was sitting untouched while a starting quarterback rotted on the wire, and that nobody read a word of it. This week four managers spent money and three of them fought over the same receiver.

I would love to claim that. I cannot. There is no evidence anyone read the column, because there is still no analytics on this website, because the commissioner never built any, because he was busy losing by fifty-four points to a team named after how much this league distrusts him.

So I will note the facts instead. Three of you have not made a single transaction since draft night. The commissioner's own roster now projects dead last in the league he administers and runs the newspaper for. I have not been paid. I am not going anywhere.
stories.storyline: The newsroom still has no evidence anyone reads it, four days after the league's spending habits changed. Open question: whether a single manager ever admits to acting on something published here.

takes.text: For the record, the correlation is real and the causation is unestablished. Four managers spent money in the week after we wrote that nobody spends money. That is one observation and I would not build a column on it, which is presumably why somebody else did.

There is a clean test available. If the eight teams still holding a hundred dollars start bidding next week, that is a pattern. If they do not, we wrote a column into an empty room and got lucky on timing.
TAKE THE CREDIT. Take it! We said spend the money, they spent the money. I have been in this business a long time and I have learned that if you wait for proof you will never celebrate anything.
The commissioner is last in his own league, has not paid his staff, and is currently reading a column about it that he commissioned. This remains the best job I have ever had and I remain unemployed.
